summary.text: A 63-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism, hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, nephrolithiasis and cholelithiasis and no previous thyroid eye disease developed right retro-orbital pain and ipsilateral hemicranial headache 3 days after a third COVID-19 vaccine dose (mRNA-1273, Moderna), having previously received two doses of the AstraZeneca vaccine.

She had grade I obesity and mildly elevated blood pressure, bilateral exophthalmos more marked on the right, eyelid retraction of 2 mm and no diplopia. Laboratory tests, orbital CT with bilateral exophthalmos and right predominance, and thyroid ultrasound with a diffuse hypoechoic goiter led the ophthalmology team to diagnose thyroid eye disease; its severity is described differently in the text and Table 1.

She received intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg weekly for 6 doses, followed by 250 mg weekly for 6 additional doses. At the 3-month follow-up she was asymptomatic (Table 1: asymptomatic at 4 months). The text also reports thyroid function tests and acute-phase reactants within normal ranges, continuation of her baseline treatments and initiation of a gradual taper of oral corticosteroids.

She complained of frontal headache, bilateral eye pain, goiter and upper limb tremors.

TED was classified as severe with grade 4 exophthalmos.

Intravenous corticosteroids were given for 12 weeks, 500 mg weekly for 6 doses then 250 mg weekly for 6 additional doses. Ophthalmologic follow-up documented a 4 mm reduction in exophthalmos and improvement from severe to moderate TED, and intramuscular corticosteroid 1 mL monthly for three months was subsequently prescribed. At the 3-month internal medicine follow-up she was hemodynamically stable and clinically improved; laboratory tests showed recovery of thyroid function.

summary.text: A 27-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism, under internal medicine control and on levothyroxine, with no previous thyroid eye disease presented 18 days after the second dose of a COVID-19 vaccine (BNT162b2, Pfizer–BioNTech). She reported weakness, drowsiness and low mood.

Physical examination was unremarkable and ophthalmologic evaluation identified mild right-sided exophthalmos. Laboratory tests showed low TSH, normal Anti-TPO, Anti-Tg and TRAb and elevated CRP. Orbital CT showed rectus muscle enlargement with unchanged oblique muscles, consistent with mild TED, and thyroid ultrasound was compatible with chronic thyroiditis.

Treatment included selenium supplementation and reduction of the levothyroxine dose. At the 3-month follow-up thyroid function had normalized, ESR remained unchanged and CRP was slightly elevated, although Table 1 says inflammatory markers were normal. Selenium and levothyroxine therapy continued due to persistent, although mild, exophthalmos.

summary.text: A 69-year-old woman with hypothyroidism, previous multinodular goiter and grade I obesity, without prior thyroid eye disease, presented 19 days after a third COVID-19 vaccine dose (BNT162b2, Pfizer–BioNTech) with neck pain, odynophagia, headache and fever (39 °C per Table 1). She was initially diagnosed with tonsillitis in the emergency department and received empirical treatment.

Four days after initiating therapy her pain improved but she developed mild bilateral exophthalmos; examination also showed obesity, normal vital signs by the text and a tender goiter. She had low TSH, elevated Anti-TPO, increased ESR and CRP, orbital CT with bilateral orbitopathy and rectus muscle enlargement, a multinodular goiter classified as TIRADS 2, and scintigraphy with 1% uptake consistent with a hypofunctioning goiter and subacute thyroiditis.

Management consisted of intramuscular corticosteroids and oral analgesics. At the 3-month follow-up the text reports slightly decreased TSH and free T4, persistently elevated ESR and CRP, elevated Anti-TPO and TRAb and persistent mild exophthalmos; Table 1 reports partial improvement at 4 months and, at 1 year, an asymptomatic patient with normal thyroid function and antibodies and a small nodular goiter with chronic thyroiditis on ultrasound.

article_limitations: Table 1 values are recorded without a time because its caption mixes baseline and outcome characteristics; times are kept only where a cell or sentence states them.

Where the case text classifies a result (normal, elevated, low) and the Table 1 value lies outside its printed reference interval, the text flag and the table value are separate included facts, the table value carries no flag, and an ambiguity records the discrepancy; flags are never derived from intervals.

Source conflicts (review-only, conflicting attribute only): Case 3 exophthalmos laterality at presentation (bilateral vs unilateral left), TED severity (moderate-to-severe vs mild) and 3-month thyroid function (free T4 slightly below normal vs thyroid function normalized); Case 4 inflammatory markers at follow-up (CRP slightly elevated vs normal). Case 1 severity (moderate-to-severe vs moderate) and the 3-month vs 4-month follow-up statements of Cases 1 and 5 are recorded as ambiguities, not conflicts.

Table 1 names products (ChAdOx1 nCoV-19, prednisone, methylprednisolone) that differ from the text wording (AstraZeneca vaccine, oral corticosteroids, corticosteroids); equivalence is not asserted except for the case 2 intravenous corticosteroid regimen, whose doses are identical.
Statements that vaccination history was obtained from the patient and confirmed from medical records have no clinical section and are not recorded as facts.

Discussion, limitations and conclusion paragraphs describe the series; counts such as numbers of patients with a finding were not copied to individuals. Figure 1 shows photographs with black rectangles over the eyes; the caption-level statement of improvement is not recorded as an individual fact.
The retrospective CAS estimates and the Table 2 group outcomes are assigned to the patients whose numbers the source lists, taking patient N as Case N (recorded as an ambiguity per patient).
